title: 9 Educational Software Companies Your District Should Know
summary: Explore top educational software companies for K-12 school districts across different areas. Learn what to look for when researching different providers.
body_markdown:
The K-12 technology landscape keeps getting more complex. With new tools launching every year, district leaders are thinking carefully about which educational software companies to partner with. The best solutions address district priorities, integrate with existing systems, support educators in their daily work, and ultimately improve student outcomes.


In this article, we’ll answer common questions about educational software companies, explore top providers serving K-12 districts, and share what to look for as you choose the right partners for your team.


## Frequently Asked Questions About Educational Software Companies


### What are educational software companies?


Educational software companies build digital tools that support teaching, learning, and school operations. In K-12, that includes everything from the platforms teachers use to plan lessons and assign work to the systems district leaders use to track attendance, monitor student progress, and plan interventions.


### What types of educational software do districts use?


Most districts use a mix of tools that serve different purposes. Common categories include:


- **Student data and**


[MTSS](https://www.panoramaed.com/solutions/mtss-software-platform) **.**


These platforms bring together academic, attendance, and behavior data so educators can identify students who need support and track interventions over time.


- **Assessment.**


Assessment tools measure what students know through screeners, diagnostic tests, and quick formative checks.


- **Curriculum and instruction.**


These programs deliver core and intervention lessons, often with built-in digital practice for students.


- **Learning management systems (LMS).**


An LMS gives teachers a place to organize assignments, grades, and class materials.


- **Family communication.**


Communication tools keep families informed through messaging and announcements.


-


[College and career readiness](https://www.panoramaed.com/solutions/graduation-career-readiness) **.**


These platforms help students track their progress toward graduation and explore options after high school.


- **Accessibility.**


Accessibility tools support students with disabilities and English language learners through features like text-to-speech and word prediction.


- **AI platforms.**


AI tools help educators analyze information, plan targeted student supports, personalize instruction, and provide timely feedback to students.


### How much does educational software cost?


The cost of educational software varies widely by product, district size, and pricing model. Companies may charge per student, per school, or through a districtwide license.


However, the license fee is only part of the picture. As you budget, also consider:


- **Implementation.**


Setup, data integration, and rostering can add upfront time and cost.


- **Training.**


Teachers may need targeted training to use new tools well, both at launch and over time.


- **Staff time.**


Someone has to manage the tool, support users, and review the data it produces.


- **Switching costs.**


Moving to a new platform later would mean migrating data and retraining staff.


Many districts fund software through federal sources such as Title I and Title IV-A, as well as state grants and general funds. Check with your federal programs director to confirm which uses are allowable.


### What should districts look for in educational software?


The best educational software fits your district’s goals, protects student data, and actually gets used. As you compare options, look for:


- **Evidence of impact.**


Look for research demonstrating the software's effectiveness, including ESSA-aligned evidence where applicable, and request results from districts like yours.


- **Data privacy.**


Evaluate the provider's FERPA and COPPA practices, review independent security assessments such as SOC 2 Type II, and confirm that the vendor can meet your district's data privacy requirements. For AI tools, ask how student data is stored, protected, and used, including whether it is used to train AI models.


- **Integration with existing tools.**


Make sure the software connects with your student information system (SIS), LMS, and rostering tools.


- **Implementation support.**


Look for hands-on onboarding and ongoing professional development offerings.


- **Total cost.**


Weigh the full cost of ownership, not just the license fee.

## 9 Educational Software Companies to Know


From student support and assessment to curriculum and instruction, K-12 software serves a wide range of district needs. Here are nine providers to know and what each brings to the table.


### 1. Panorama Education


[Panorama Education](https://www.panoramaed.com/) helps K-12 districts see the whole picture of every student. Its platform brings academics, attendance, behavior, graduation progress, and student voice into one connected view, so educators can quickly understand what’s happening, why it matters, and what to do next. Today, Panorama partners with more than 2,000 districts serving over 15 million students nationwide.


#### Top offerings


-


[Panorama Student Success](https://www.panoramaed.com/products/student-success) **.**


This MTSS platform brings together data on academics, coursework, attendance, behavior, life skills, and graduation in one place. Your educators can see at a glance which students are on track and which need support, rather than piecing together information from separate systems. Then, they can plan targeted interventions and track how students respond over time.


-


[Panorama Solara](https://www.panoramaed.com/products/solara) **.**


Solara is an AI tool that draws on your district’s data, policies, and practices, so its output reflects your students and community. Educators can use prebuilt tools within Solara to draft intervention plans, attendance plans, behavior plans, progress reports, and special education documents, as well as lesson plans, rubrics, and leveled texts. Your district can also build custom AI tools from your own approved materials and track how staff use AI across the district. Student data is not used to train AI models, and the platform meets SOC 2, FERPA, and COPPA standards.


-


[Panorama Pathways](https://www.panoramaed.com/products/pathways) **.**


Students and counselors can track progress toward graduation and explore career and technical education (CTE) and workforce pathways in one place. The platform lightens the time-consuming work of auditing, reporting, and updating transcripts and schedules, so counselors can spend more time guiding students toward life after high school.


-


[Panorama Surveys and Engagement](https://www.panoramaed.com/products/surveys) **.**


Your district can gather feedback from students, families, and staff on the topics that matter most to their community, from school climate to family engagement. Then, your school and district leaders can use the results to understand what’s working, spot areas for growth, and guide school improvement plans with input from the people they serve.


#### What this provider does best


Panorama connects data to action. Instead of switching between disconnected systems, educators get a complete picture of each student. That means less time searching for information and more time giving students the support they need. Hands-on professional development then helps teams put it all into practice.


### 2. Google for Education


[Google for Education](https://edu.google.com/intl/ALL_us/) provides the everyday tools many classrooms run on, from Google Classroom to Chromebooks. Its familiar, cloud-based tools make it easy for teachers and students to create, share, and collaborate from any device.


#### Top offerings


- **Google Classroom.**


Teachers can manage assignments, grading, and class communication in one place.


- **Google Workspace for Education.**


This suite includes Gmail, Drive, Docs, Calendar, and Meet, with editions for different district needs.


- **Gemini for Education.**


Google’s AI tool helps educators plan lessons, personalize learning, and handle administrative tasks.


- **Chromebooks.**


These fast, easy-to-use laptops give students reliable access to their classwork, research, and digital learning tools at school or at home.


#### What this provider does best


Google for Education stands out for its ease of use. Because many teachers and students are already familiar with its tools, districts may face a shorter learning curve when introducing them. This also makes Google a common foundation for other software to connect to.


### 3. Microsoft for Education


[Microsoft for Education](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education) brings the familiar Microsoft 365 apps into classrooms, along with learning tools that support reading, accessibility, and collaboration.


#### Top offerings


- **Microsoft 365 Education.**


Students and staff get Word, PowerPoint, OneNote, Excel, and other core apps.


- **Microsoft Teams for Education.**


Teachers can run virtual classrooms for assignments, meetings, and collaboration.


- **Learning Accelerators.**


Tools such as Reading Progress help students build reading fluency and other foundational skills.


- **Minecraft Education.**


This game-based platform helps teachers bring subjects from coding to history to life.


- **Microsoft Copilot.**


Copilot brings AI assistance to everyday Microsoft 365 apps, helping educators save time and focus more on their students.


#### What this provider does best


Microsoft for Education is a strong fit for districts already running on Microsoft systems. Its built-in learning and accessibility tools help make content more accessible to students with diverse learning needs.


### 4. Curriculum Associates


[Curriculum Associates](https://www.curriculumassociates.com/) is best known for i-Ready, an assessment and instruction program used in classrooms nationwide. The company pairs diagnostic data with curriculum to help teachers meet students where they are in reading and math.


#### Top offerings


- **i-Ready Assessment.**


Diagnostic assessments show where each student stands in reading and math.


- **i-Ready Personalized Instruction.**


Online lessons adjust to each student’s diagnostic results.


- **i-Ready Classroom Mathematics.**


This core math curriculum includes built-in teacher support.


- **Magnetic Literacy and Ready Reading.**


These literacy programs focus on reading comprehension and foundational skills.


- **Ellevation.**


Ellevation combines student data and research-based instructional strategies to help educators support English language learners.


#### What this provider does best


Curriculum Associates excels at connecting assessment to instruction. Teachers can move directly from diagnostic results to lessons matched to each student’s needs, making it easier to differentiate in reading and math.


### 5. HMH


[HMH (Houghton Mifflin Harcourt)](https://www.hmhco.com/) is one of the largest K-12 curriculum providers in the U.S. Through its digital learning platform, HMH Ed, teachers can access core and intervention programs across literacy, math, science, and social studies, along with online assessments from its


[NWEA (Northwest Evaluation Association) division](https://www.nwea.org/) .


#### Top offerings


- **HMH Ed.**


This online platform brings HMH’s curriculum, assessments, and teaching resources together in one place, so teachers can plan lessons, assign work, and track student progress.


- **Into Reading and Into Literature.**


These core literacy programs for grades K-12 include digital lessons, interactive texts, and online practice.


- **Into Math.**


This core math curriculum runs from kindergarten through Algebra 1, with digital lessons and adaptive practice that adjust to each student’s needs.


- **Read 180 and Math 180.**


These intervention programs use adaptive software to meet students at their level and help them catch up in reading and math.


- **NWEA®**


***MAP***


**®**


***Growth***


**™.**


These online assessments measure student growth over time.


- **Writable.**


This online writing program gives students in grades 3-12 practice and instant feedback on their writing.


#### What this provider does best


HMH offers breadth. Districts can access core curriculum, intervention programs, and assessments from a single provider, with professional learning to support implementation.


### 6. Newsela


[Newsela](https://newsela.com/) is known for turning real-world news and texts into engaging lessons at multiple reading levels. Over time, it has grown into a broader instruction and assessment platform used by more than 1,000 districts.


#### Top offerings


- **Newsela ELA, Social Studies, and STEM.**


A library of more than 18,000 texts and videos that gives teachers content at different reading levels.


- **Newsela Writing.**


Students build writing skills through instruction and practice tied to Newsela content.


- **Balanced Assessment by Formative.**


Teachers can check for understanding in real time and act on the results.


- **Luna.**


This AI teaching assistant helps with lesson planning, activity design, and text differentiation.


#### What this provider does best


Newsela makes rigorous, relevant content accessible to every reader. Because each text comes in multiple reading levels, students can engage with the same material as their classmates while building literacy skills across subjects.


### 7. ClassDojo


[ClassDojo](https://www.classdojo.com/) connects teachers, students, and families through a suite of tools for classroom community, communication, and learning. Its core app is free for teachers, and over the years, ClassDojo has grown to include products that support learning at home as well.


#### Top offerings


- **ClassDojo.**


The core app helps teachers build a positive classroom culture and keep families in the loop. Teachers can share photos and updates through classroom Stories, message families with automatic translation into more than 190 languages, recognize students with points, and collect student work in digital portfolios.


- **ClassDojo Plus.**


This optional paid subscription gives families extra features, including progress reports, scheduled and read-receipt messaging, interactive books, and a homework helper that walks students through problems step by step without giving away the answers.


- **Dojo Islands.**


This play-based learning world lets kids explore STEM, creativity, and teamwork together, both in the classroom and at home.


- **Dojo Tutor.**


Families can book personalized, one-on-one online tutoring with certified teachers in subjects like math and reading.


- **Dojo Sparks.**


This early reading app uses speech recognition to listen as young children sound out letters and words. It gives real-time feedback on phonics, blending, rhyming, and vocabulary in short, 15-minute lessons.


#### What this provider does best


ClassDojo excels at bringing teachers and families together. Its simple, multilingual communication tools make it easy for every family to stay involved, and its growing set of learning products helps that connection carry over from the classroom to home.


### 8. Seesaw


[Seesaw](https://seesaw.com/) is a learning platform built for elementary school students. It gives young learners simple, creative ways to show what they know and lets families follow their child’s progress.


#### Top offerings


- **Elementary LMS.**


Teachers in grades K-6 can manage assignments and student portfolios in one place.


- **Instruction and Insights.**


Standards-based reporting helps teachers track student progress.


- **Seesaw AI.**


AI tools help teachers create activities, differentiate instruction, and check for understanding.


- **Supplemental curriculum.**


Programs cover writing, early literacy, computer science, and English language development.


#### What this provider does best


Seesaw is designed around how young children learn. Students can draw, record audio or video, and snap photos to show their thinking, giving teachers and families a fuller picture than a worksheet can.


### 9. Everway


[Everway](https://www.everway.com/education/) (formerly Texthelp) creates tools that make learning accessible for every student. Its software supports students with disabilities, English language learners, and anyone who needs extra reading and writing support.


#### Top offerings


- **Read&Write.**


This literacy toolbar offers text-to-speech, word prediction, and other reading and writing supports, and it’s free for K-12 teachers.


- **Equatio.**


Students can type, speak, or handwrite equations, making math more accessible.


- **OrbitNote.**


OrbitNote turns PDFs into accessible, interactive documents.


- **Unique Learning System.**


This standards-aligned special education curriculum spans pre-K through transition.


#### What this provider does best


Everway removes barriers to learning. Its tools work inside the platforms students already use, including Google Classroom, Microsoft 365, and Canvas, so accessibility supports are always within reach.


## How to Choose an Educational Software Company to Partner With: 8 Steps


Knowing which educational software companies are out there is only half the battle. The harder part is deciding which ones deserve a place in your district.


Each new tool affects teachers’ workloads, students’ experiences, and how well your systems work together, so a thoughtful vetting process will pay off long after the contract is signed. These eight steps can help you evaluate options with confidence.


### 1. Define the problem you’re solving.


Start with student needs and district goals. For instance, are you trying to reduce chronic absenteeism, improve reading outcomes, or lighten the paperwork that keeps teachers from their students? Naming the problems first gives your team a clear way to judge every option.


A clear goal also keeps you from buying tools that look impressive in a demo but won’t move the needle. Write down what success looks like before you talk to a single vendor, so you can measure each product against it.


### 2. Take stock of what tools you already have.


Before adding anything new to your tech stack, audit the software your district already uses. For each tool, note:


- What it does


- Who uses it and how often


- What it costs each year


- Whether it overlaps with another tool


This review can save your district time and money, as you may be able to expand a tool you already pay for or replace several disconnected tools with one platform that does more.


### 3. Bring the right people to the table.


Involve key stakeholders early in the process. Each group brings a different perspective:


- **Teachers**


know what works in the classroom and what will actually get used.


- **IT staff**


know which tools will fit your existing tech stack and security requirements.


- **Curriculum leaders**


can make sure a tool supports your district’s instructional goals.


- **Finance teams**


can flag long-term costs and funding options.


- **Students and families,**


when it makes sense, can share how a tool affects them day to day.


Bringing people in from the start also builds buy-in. For example, when educators help choose a tool, they’re more likely to use it and champion it during rollout.


### 4. Check the evidence.


Look for research demonstrating the software's effectiveness, including ESSA-aligned evidence where applicable. Ask vendors to share studies, measurable outcomes, and examples from districts similar to yours. Customer references can also offer valuable perspective on how a solution performs in practice.


### 5. Review their data privacy and security measures.


Protecting student data should be non-negotiable. Before signing on, confirm that the vendor:


- Complies with FERPA, COPPA, and your state’s student privacy laws


- Will sign your district’s data privacy agreement


- Provides independent security assessments, such as a SOC 2 Type II report


- Limits who can access student information


- Explains how it stores and protects student data


- Guarantees in writing that student data won’t be used to train AI models (for any tool that includes AI)


### 6. Make sure any new tools work with your existing ones.


When your tools don’t talk to each other, student information ends up scattered across separate systems. For instance, a counselor might see attendance data in one place, while a teacher tracks grades in another. That makes it harder to:


- **See the full picture.**


No one has a complete view of how a student is doing across academics, attendance, and behavior.


- **Spot students who need help.**


Warning signs get missed when the data that would reveal them lives in different places.


- **Act quickly.**


Educators lose valuable time logging into multiple platforms and piecing information together by hand.


To avoid creating additional data silos, ask vendors whether their product connects with your SIS, LMS, and rostering tools. When the tools share data with the systems you already use, educators can spend less time searching for information and more time supporting students.


### 7. Look at the total cost and customer support.


Look beyond the license fee to the full cost of ownership, including implementation, training, staff time, and the cost of switching platforms later. A lower-priced tool can end up costing more if it requires heavy setup or ongoing troubleshooting.


Ask what onboarding, professional development, and ongoing support the vendor includes. How well a tool is rolled out often matters as much as the tool itself, so look for a partner that will work alongside your team long after launch.


### 8. Pilot the tool and gather results.


When feasible, pilot the tool or evaluate its performance in comparable districts. A pilot can help your team understand how a solution works in practice, while customer references, case studies, and implementation discussions can provide valuable evidence when a pilot isn't practical.


Set clear success measures up front, such as:


- **Usage rates.**


Are teachers and students using the tool regularly?


- **Teacher feedback.**


Does it save time or make their work easier?


- **Student outcomes.**


Are you seeing progress toward the goals you set?


Review the results with district leaders before deciding to expand, adjust, or move on. A thoughtful pilot reduces risk and gives you the evidence you need to make the case to your school board.
